Monday. Keerthana called from the hospital corridor, sobbing: her mother's surgery had been moved up. Ayesha felt her own heart start to race. She sat down, took three slow breaths, and let her voice come out warm and steady. 'I'm here. What would help most right now?' Keerthana thought. 'Could you pick up Amma's glasses from home?'
Wednesday. Ayesha dropped off the glasses and a tiffin, sat with Keerthana for an hour, then went home and slept, phone on silent, as she'd promised herself.
The following Sunday. Keerthana's mother was home. Ayesha, rested, came with flowers, and laughed with them for the first time in a week.

qa.a: Amma's glasses from home.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when her heart started to race, and what did she do with it?

passage: Gurleen, you asked how I've lasted thirty years on the ambulance. Let me tell you about when I was twenty-four. First big accident on the highway: a boy trapped in a car, his mother screaming. I felt everything she felt. I shook so hard I dropped the kit. My senior, old Mathew sir, gripped my shoulder. 'Kishore. Breathe. Slowly. Now: what does this boy need from you?' I breathed. My hands steadied. I still cared, oh, I cared, but I wasn't drowning with her. After that shift he made me eat, sit in the sun, and sleep. 'A tired heart helps nobody,' he said. So I tell you the same. Breathe, ask what will help, then go home and rest.

qa.q: Who gripped Kishore's shoulder at the accident?
qa.a: Old Mathew sir, the senior.

qa.q: How did young Kishore feel after breathing slowly?
qa.a: Kishore's hands steadied; the caring stayed, but Kishore was no longer drowning in the mother's panic.

qa.q: Which part of Mathew sir's lesson helps care last thirty years, and why?
qa.a: Resting after hard shifts matters as much as breathing, because a tired heart can't keep helping others.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen need to hear this now?
qa.a: Gurleen, probably newer to ambulance work, may be feeling the same shaking and exhaustion, and could use a practical way through it.

grounding: An elder paramedic recalls learning at twenty-four to breathe, ask what would help, and rest so care can last.

passage: The office Diwali party was deafening: speakers, crackers outside, fifty people shouting over each other. Zubin found Afreen in the stairwell, phone at two percent, shaking. 'Abbu's had an accident. They've taken him to the hospital in Thane. I can't think.' Zubin's own chest tightened. He sat on the step beside her and breathed out, slowly, twice, until his hands were still. 'Okay. I'm here. What would help most right now?' 'I need to get there. My phone's dying.' He handed her his power bank, booked a cab, and called her brother so she could talk while they waited. He rode with her to the hospital gate. At midnight, once her brother arrived, Zubin went home, drank some water and slept. He would check on her in the morning, rested.

Preeti was halfway through her coffee at the co-working space in Indiranagar when Jagdish, from the next desk, put his phone down and went grey. "They've let me go. Just an email. Eight of us."
His hands were shaking. Preeti felt her own chest tighten, as if the email had been hers too. She set the cup down, let out a long slow breath, then another, and felt her shoulders drop.
"That's awful, Jagdish," she said, and meant it. "What would help right now? Air? Someone to sit with you? Or should I call someone?"
"Just... sit for a bit."
So she sat. Later she walked with him to the auto stand and messaged to check he got home.
That night she wanted to keep texting him till midnight. Instead she sent one message, "Here tomorrow if you want to talk," and went to bed early. She had a long week ahead, and he would need her in it.

qa.q: How did Jagdish learn he had been let go?
qa.a: Just an email.

qa.q: What did Preeti feel when she heard Jagdish's news, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: Her chest tightened as if the news were hers, but she took long slow breaths until her shoulders dropped and she could feel warm concern instead of panic.

qa.q: Why was asking 'What would help right now?' a good choice?
qa.a: It let Jagdish decide what he needed, so Preeti could give real help, just sitting with him, instead of guessing or taking over.

qa.q: How might Jagdish experience Preeti's calm presence?
qa.a: He probably felt steadier having someone quiet beside him and knowing she would be there tomorrow too, rather than someone as shaken as he was.

"Didi, are you awake?" Sameer stood in the doorway at midnight, eyes red.
Rupali put down her phone. "Now I am. Come."
He sat on the edge of her bed. "I didn't clear the entrance. Again. Papa's going to..." His voice broke.
Rupali's stomach dropped. She wanted to cry with him. Instead she breathed in slowly, out slowly, twice. "Okay. I'm here."
"Everyone will ask."
"They will. What would help tonight? Talking, or not talking?"
"Not talking. Just... don't go."
"I'll make chai."
They drank it on her bed while he scrolled nothing. At one she said, "Sameer, I have a six a.m. shift. I need to sleep, or I'll be useless to you tomorrow. Breakfast together? We'll plan what to tell Papa."
He nodded. "Breakfast."
"And wake me if it gets bad."

qa.a: At midnight.

qa.q: What did Rupali want to do when she heard Sameer's news, and what does her breathing show?
qa.a: She wanted to cry with him; breathing slowly shows she chose to steady herself first so she could stay with him calmly.

qa.q: Why was Rupali's decision to sleep at one o'clock a wise one?
qa.a: She knew she needed rest to be useful the next day, and she still left Sameer with a plan for breakfast and permission to wake her.

qa.a: He might feel a little alone at first, but the breakfast plan and 'wake me if it gets bad' tell him she is not leaving him with it.

passage:
I'm Pema. Preeti called me at ten last night, crying so hard I couldn't understand her at first. Her job offer had been withdrawn, the day before she was supposed to join.
I felt my chest go tight, like her panic was climbing into me. That's what usually happens. I end up crying with her and we both spiral.
This time I put my feet flat on the floor and breathed out slowly, twice. Then I said, "I'm here. I'm listening." And after a while, "What would help you right now?"
She said, "Just stay on the phone while I make tea." So I did.
At eleven thirty I told her, "I need to sleep so I can be useful tomorrow. Can I come over after work?" She said yes.
I slept. I went. We made a list together.

qa.a: At ten at night.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when the chest went tight?
qa.a: Pema felt Preeti's panic rising inside, worried they would both spiral, and then steadied with slow breaths.

qa.q: Which choices worked, and why?

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt when Pema asked what would help?
qa.a: She probably felt listened to and a little calmer, able to ask for something simple like company while making tea.

Supervisor's note, community centre, Wednesday.
A young woman, Bidisha, came in this afternoon very distressed; her landlord had told her to leave by the weekend. She was shaking and talking fast.
Manjula, our new caseworker, met her in the front room. I watched from the door. I saw Manjula's own face tighten for a moment. Then she sat down, put both feet on the floor, and took two slow breaths before speaking.
She kept her voice low. "That sounds frightening. What would help most today?" Bidisha said a place to stay for two nights. Manjula made two calls and found a hostel bed.
At six, when Manjula would usually stay late, I saw her pack up. She said, "I'll be better for her tomorrow if I sleep tonight."
What I did next: I gave Manjula the follow-up slot tomorrow morning and told her I'd noticed how steady she was.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say would help most?
qa.a: A place to stay for two nights.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when her face tightened?
qa.a: She felt Bidisha's fear catch in her, and then steadied herself with slow breaths.

qa.q: What did Manjula do well, and why does it matter for her work?
qa.a: She settled first, asked what would help, found a hostel bed and went home to rest, so her care stays steady and lasts.

qa.a: She probably felt less panicked and more hopeful as someone steady focused on what would help.

passage:
Monday night
Elizabeth came home at eight and burst into tears in the kitchen. Her grandmother was in hospital in Shillong, and she couldn't get a flight till Thursday.
My first feeling was my own stomach twisting. I nearly started crying too, like I always do.
Instead I stopped. Two slow breaths. Hands on the counter. I told myself: this is her fear, I can hold it without drowning in it.
I asked, "What would help right now?" She said, "Honestly? Tea. And help looking at trains." So we did that. I made tea, and we found a train for tomorrow night.
At eleven she wanted to keep talking, and I said gently, "I need sleep, so I can drive you to the station tomorrow." She hugged me.
Going to bed. Feeling tired, but okay.
– Neelam

qa.a: In Shillong.

qa.a: Neelam felt a twist of worry and nearly cried too, then settled with two slow breaths.

passage:
When the flood water went into Jeevan's house in the village near Kottayam, he stood in the mud of his front room and did not speak.
Kashish, who ran the dairy co-op office, came by that afternoon. She felt her stomach drop at the sight of his soaked rice sacks. She stopped at the gate, took three slow breaths, and walked in.
"Jeevan chetta, what would help today?"
He pointed at the drowned hens. "I can't even start."
"Then let's start small. Dry things first."
She sent two boys for dry sacks, sat with him while he made a list, and called the panchayat office about relief.
At dusk she went home, ate, and went to bed early. "Tomorrow again," she told him. "I'll be more use rested."

qa.q: What did Kashish send the two boys to get?
qa.a: She sent them for dry sacks.

qa.q: What did Kashish feel when she saw Jeevan's soaked rice sacks?
qa.a: She felt her stomach drop in shock and sadness, but she steadied herself with slow breaths so her concern stayed warm and useful.

qa.q: Which of Kashish's choices help care last over the coming days?
qa.a: Asking what would help, starting small with dry things, calling the panchayat office, and going home to rest so she can return tomorrow.

passage:
Dear Akash,

You asked how I manage at the children's hospital without falling apart. Honestly, I didn't at first. In my first months as a play therapist, I felt every child's fear as if it were mine and went home shaking. Now I do something different. Before I walk into a room, I stop at the door and take three slow breaths. I remind myself: this is their fear, I can hold their hand without drowning in it. Then I ask the child or the parent, 'What would help right now?' Sometimes it's a game, sometimes a hug, sometimes just quiet. And on weekends I sleep, cook and see friends, because tired carers aren't good carers. I care just as much. I just last longer.

Warmly,
Devika

qa.a: Three slow breaths.

qa.q: How did Devika feel in the first months at the hospital?
qa.a: Devika felt every child's fear as if it were Devika's own and went home shaking.

qa.q: What in Devika's routine helps the care last?
qa.a: Breathing before each room, separating the child's fear from Devika's own, asking what would help, and resting at weekends.

qa.q: How might a child in the hospital experience Devika's calm approach?
qa.a: A child is likely to feel safer and listened to, since Devika asks what would help instead of panicking too.

passage: Rashmi, you asked on the podcast how I work in disaster relief without burning out. I'm Yogesh, and I nearly did. In my first flood, I merged with everyone's pain. I cried with every family and couldn't sleep. By day four I was useless. My team leader pulled me aside. She said, 'Your panic doesn't help them. Your steadiness does.' So now I have a routine. Before I sit with a family, I slow my breathing, feel my feet on the ground. I let myself feel warm concern, but I don't try to feel exactly what they feel. Then I ask, 'What would help you most today?' Usually it's water, a phone call, or just someone to write down names. And every night, no matter what, I sleep six hours. Care has to last.

qa.q: How long does Yogesh sleep every night now?
qa.a: Six hours, no matter what.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel by day four of the first flood?
qa.a: Yogesh felt overwhelmed, exhausted and useless, having merged with everyone's pain.

qa.q: Which part of Yogesh's routine helps the families most?
qa.a: Asking 'What would help you most today?' from a steady place, which leads to practical help like water or phone calls.

qa.q: How might the team leader have seen Yogesh on day four?
qa.a: She saw that his panic wasn't helping and cared enough to pull him aside and teach steadiness.

grounding: An adult learns to settle the breath, feel concern without merging, ask what would help, and protect rest so care can last.

I share the flat with Tenzin and Jomon, so I was there when Jomon's phone rang at eleven that night. His father had been taken to hospital in Kottayam. Jomon went grey and started pacing, talking too fast, dropping his charger twice.
Tenzin didn't jump up. I watched Tenzin set down the tea, breathe out slowly, twice, and sit on the arm of the sofa. "Jomon. What would help right now?"
"I don't know. The train, I think. A ticket."
So they did that. Tenzin found a seat on the 5 a.m. train and packed Jomon's bag while Jomon talked to his sister.
At one, I saw Tenzin set an alarm for four and go to bed. "If I'm wrecked tomorrow, I'm no use to him," Tenzin said. I can't say what Tenzin felt, but the flat was calmer for it.
